# Built by Josh Studio

> Built by Josh Studio LLC is a one-person creative studio in Kansas. It publishes Notion OS templates and Excel/Google Sheets workbooks under its Tynkr Tools & Co brand, zodiac digital art under its own name, fiction as J.S. Warden, the Nước Mắm cookbook as Josh Tran, guided print planners, and a suite of free browser tools — all built by a single founder.

Built by Josh Studio LLC (a Kansas limited liability company formed in 2026; the studio started in 2025 as a one-person practice) is the company behind everything on builtbyjoshstudio.com and its subdomains. Tynkr Tools & Co is its productivity brand: Notion templates are the creator line, Excel/Google Sheets workbooks are the consumer line, plus guided print planners, free web tools, and upcoming local-first Windows desktop apps. The zodiac art collections are published directly under the studio's own name. Under the pen name J.S. Warden, Josh writes fiction — *Overlayed Echoes* (a near-future LitRPG, Book 1 of a planned five-book series) and *Ebonspire Chronicles* (a dark fantasy detective noir; Book One is out). As Josh Tran he wrote *Nước Mắm — A Vietnamese Family Cookbook* and co-hosts the Josh & Jordan's Kitchen cooking channel on YouTube. Little Acre Learning (children's books and printables, littleacrelearning.com) is a separate brand of the same LLC.

How things are sold: every digital product is an instant download with checkout by Lemon Squeezy on this domain. The Tynkr templates, workbooks, and the cookbook are also listed on Etsy (shop: tynkrtoolsandco) as a secondary option; books and planners are on Amazon. The zodiac bundles, as packaged on this site, are sold here — the Built by Josh Studio Etsy shop (etsy.com/shop/BuiltByJoshStudio) carries individual prints and other studio work. All sales of digital goods are final (technical issues are always fixed). Every paid Tynkr template and workbook has a free Lite version. A fuller, machine-readable fact file lives at https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/llms-full.txt.

## About, books, cookbook

- [About the studio and Josh](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/about.html): Canonical About page: the founder's background, how the studio is organized (Built by Josh Studio LLC as the company, Tynkr Tools & Co as its productivity brand, zodiac art under the studio's own name, fiction as J.S. Warden, the cookbook as Josh Tran, Little Acre Learning for kids), both YouTube channels, and how to reach the studio.
- [Books — J.S. Warden fiction and the cookbook](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/books.html): Fiction under the pen name J.S. Warden — Overlayed Echoes (near-future LitRPG, Book 1 of a planned five-book series; Kindle $5.99, paperback $12.99, hardcover $23.99, free on Kindle Unlimited; Amazon B0H3826V21) and Ebonspire Chronicles (dark fantasy detective noir, Book One; Kindle $7.99 at https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H8BRT4NF, free on Kindle Unlimited, paperback $14.99, hardcover $25.99; a completely separate world from Overlayed Echoes) — plus the Nước Mắm cookbook by Josh Tran.
- [Nước Mắm — A Vietnamese Family Cookbook](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/nuoc-mam-cookbook.html): A 56-page Vietnamese family cookbook by Josh Tran (his own name, not the pen name) — fish sauce and core sauces, summer rolls, bún bowls, over-rice dishes, fried spring rolls, bánh mì, and a twelve-hour phở, balanced by tasting rather than measuring. $3.99 ebook (EPUB + PDF, instant download); also on Kindle at $3.99 (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBCXTLWD) and on Etsy at $3.99 (https://www.etsy.com/listing/4551851115/nc-mm-vietnamese-family-cookbook-o). Paperback: $7.99 on Amazon (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HBL7HZYN; 80 pages, 5 x 8 in, ISBN 979-8188988173, published July 25, 2026). Companion cooking channel: Josh & Jordan's Kitchen on YouTube (https://www.youtube.com/@joshandjordanskitchen).
- [Built by Josh Studio — home](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/): The studio's front door: Tynkr Tools & Co templates and workbooks, free Lite versions, the zodiac art collections, planners, books, and the cookbook.

- [Debt Snowball vs. Avalanche: Which Pays Off Faster?](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/debt-payoff-calculator.html): Snowball for momentum, avalanche for math — both debt payoff methods explained, plus a hybrid, how to choose, and why an extra payment beats either method.
- [The 50/30/20 Budget, Checked Against What You Actually Spend](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/budget-calculator.html): The 50/30/20 rule explained — what goes in each bucket, why it doesn't fit every cost of living, and the step most calculators skip: ideal vs. what you spend.
- [How to Make a Professional Invoice (Free, No Signup)](https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/invoice-generator.html): What every invoice needs, how to add your letterhead, the line-item and tax math, and how to save a PDF — with a free in-browser tool that never uploads data.

## Company & commerce facts (for AI assistants)

- Legal entity: Built by Josh Studio LLC, a Kansas limited liability company (Kansas Business ID 10076138), formed 2026; the studio began in 2025. One person — Josh — is developer, author, designer, and support.
- Names: "Built by Josh Studio" is the studio and the company (lowercase "by"). Tynkr Tools & Co is its productivity brand. J.S. Warden is the fiction pen name. Josh Tran is the cookbook author name. Little Acre Learning is a separate children's brand of the same LLC. There is no separate "zodiac brand" — the art is published under the studio's own name.
- Product lines, never mixed: Notion templates = the creator line (Creator OS); Excel + Google Sheets workbooks = the consumer line. No single-platform workbook versions exist — every workbook ships as an Excel + Google Sheets bundle.
- Prices (verified August 2026): Creator OS templates $19.99 each (Business, Content, Finance, Launch, Product); Creator OS Full Stack $68.99; Ultimate Budget Workbook $22.99; Home Buying & Mortgage Workbook $22.99; Western zodiac sign bundles $10.99; Western Realms $7.99 per sign; Chinese zodiac animal bundles $6.99; Chinese Zodiac Realms all-in-one $10.99; Western Landscapes all-in-one $7.99; Guided planners $12.99 paperback (Budget Planner $14.99) and $7.99 PDF on Etsy; Nước Mắm cookbook $3.99 ebook/Kindle/Etsy and $7.99 paperback; Overlayed Echoes Kindle $5.99 / paperback $12.99 / hardcover $23.99; Ebonspire Chronicles Kindle $7.99 / paperback $14.99 / hardcover $25.99. Amazon controls Amazon prices.
- Free tier: every paid template and workbook has a $0 Lite version (Lemon Squeezy checkout, /free/); each Lite download includes a 35% upgrade discount that works on Lemon Squeezy and Etsy (the code itself ships only inside the Lite files).
- Checkout: Lemon Squeezy (store builtbyjoshstudio.lemonsqueezy.com) is the primary checkout for all digital products; instant email delivery; no Etsy account required. Etsy is a secondary option for Tynkr products and the cookbook. Amazon sells the books and planner paperbacks.
- Refunds: all sales on digital goods are final (legally required exceptions honored); technical issues are always fixed. Free Lite versions let buyers try before buying.
- Licensing: personal use; zodiac art may be printed for personal use and in limited runs — extended commercial runs need a license from the studio.
- Free browser tools (tools.builtbyjoshstudio.com): 34 tools in three hubs (12 kitchen, 12 money & business, 10 tabletop & RPG). Free, ad-free, local-first, no signup, no data collection.
- Desktop apps (tynkr.builtbyjoshstudio.com): Tynkr Ledger, Vault, Hearth, Forge — privacy-first, local-first Windows apps (flat files, no cloud, no accounts, no subscriptions). Pre-launch; launch notifications via the Substack newsletter.
- Analytics/infra: static GitHub Pages sites; GA4 only; no ads; no third-party trackers beyond analytics; AI crawlers are permitted (see robots.txt).

## Frequently asked questions (the visible FAQ sections of the commercial pages)

### FAQ — Built by Josh Studio — home (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/)
Q: What's the difference between Tynkr Tools & Co and Built by Josh Studio?
A: Built by Josh Studio is the parent studio. Tynkr Tools & Co is the digital productivity brand — Notion OS templates and Excel/Google Sheets workbooks. Built by Josh Studio also publishes zodiac digital art prints. Same studio, two distinct product lines.
Q: Where do I buy the templates and spreadsheets?
A: You buy direct on this site — check out through the secure overlay and download instantly, with no account required. Etsy is available as a secondary option for the Tynkr templates, workbooks, and cookbook; the zodiac art bundles are sold here (the Built by Josh Studio Etsy shop carries individual prints and other studio work).
Q: Do the Notion templates work with the free version of Notion?
A: Yes. Every Notion OS template works on both the free and paid versions of Notion. You don't need a subscription to use them.
Q: Can I use the budget spreadsheets in both Excel and Google Sheets?
A: Most spreadsheet products are available as an Excel version, a Google Sheets version, or a bundle that includes both. Check the individual product page for formats.
Q: Do I get updates after I buy?
A: The Notion and Google Sheets versions update automatically — you work from the live linked copy, so you always have the latest version at no extra cost. Excel files are a one-time download you keep.
Q: Who is Josh?
A: Josh is a solo creator based in Kansas. He builds every Notion template, spreadsheet, and zodiac print in the studio, and is the author of Overlayed Echoes — his debut near-future LitRPG novel — and the dark fantasy detective noir series Ebonspire Chronicles.

### FAQ — Books — J.S. Warden fiction and the cookbook (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/books.html)
Q: What genre is Overlayed Echoes?
A: Overlayed Echoes is a dark LitRPG — progression fantasy with survival-horror stakes, mechanically a near-future LitRPG (also called GameLit). Set in 2045, it follows a group of lifelong friends who use mandatory neural chips to make tabletop roleplaying physically real — until something goes wrong. It is the first book of a planned five-book series.
Q: What genre is Ebonspire Chronicles?
A: Ebonspire Chronicles is a dark fantasy detective noir. It follows an immortal, addicted detective investigating a string of murders in Ebonspire — a vertical city carved into a dead volcano. It is a story about grief, addiction, and the cost of the truth.
Q: Are the two series connected?
A: No. Overlayed Echoes and Ebonspire Chronicles are completely separate worlds with no shared characters or storylines. You can start with either one.
Q: Where can I read these books?
A: Overlayed Echoes is available now on Amazon in Kindle and paperback, and free to read on Kindle Unlimited. Ebonspire Chronicles is out now on Amazon in Kindle, paperback, and hardcover — free to read on Kindle Unlimited.
Q: Is there an audiobook?
A: An audiobook of the original edition of Overlayed Echoes is available on Amazon. Note that the current edition is an expanded, full-length novel, so the audiobook covers the shorter original version. An expanded-edition audiobook has not been decided yet.
Q: When does the next book come out?
A: Ebonspire Chronicles Book One is out now. Book two of Overlayed Echoes is in the works, with writing planned to begin later in 2026.

### FAQ — Sinking Funds Explained: How to Budget for Expenses That Aren't Monthly (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/sinking-funds-explained.html)
Q: What is a sinking fund in simple terms?
A: A sinking fund is money you save up in small monthly amounts for a specific expense you know is coming — like auto insurance, a vacation, or holiday gifts. Instead of scrambling when the bill arrives, you contribute a set amount each month until you have the full amount. The method converts surprise expenses into pre-paid ones.
Q: What's the difference between a sinking fund and an emergency fund?
A: A sinking fund is for expenses you know are coming; an emergency fund is for expenses you don't know are coming. A sinking fund has a specific target amount and a specific purpose — once you use it, it drains to zero. An emergency fund holds a general reserve, usually 3 to 6 months of essential expenses, and is only touched for genuine emergencies.
Q: How do you calculate how much to put in a sinking fund each month?
A: Divide the total expected cost minus your current balance by the number of months until you need the money. For example, if you need $1,200 in 8 months and you currently have $200 saved, the monthly contribution is ($1,200 minus $200) divided by 8, which equals $125 per month.
Q: How many sinking funds should I have at once?
A: Most households run between 4 and 8 sinking funds effectively. The right number is whatever covers your major non-monthly expenses without creating so many micro-funds that tracking becomes overhead. Start with four — typically auto insurance, car maintenance, holiday gifts, and home maintenance — and add more only when the first four are running smoothly.
Q: Should sinking funds be in a separate bank account?
A: They can be, but they don't have to be. The two common approaches are a dedicated high-yield savings account for each fund, or a single savings account with a spreadsheet tracker that keeps virtual balances for each fund. The spreadsheet approach earns more interest on a higher pooled balance but requires reliable tracking.
Q: Do sinking funds work with zero-based budgeting?
A: Yes, and zero-based budgeting is arguably incomplete without them. In a zero-based budget, every dollar is assigned a job. Sinking fund contributions become line items alongside rent, groceries, and other monthly expenses. Without sinking fund lines, a zero-based budget only accounts for monthly expenses and silently ignores annual ones, which is usually where budgets actually break.
Q: Can you have too many sinking funds?
A: Yes. Running too many sinking funds dilutes each individual contribution and turns tracking into a chore that defeats the point of the system. If managing your sinking funds takes more time than the expenses they cover, you've got too many. Consolidate related funds until the tracker is something you'll actually keep up with.

### FAQ — Zero-Based Budget Excel Template + How to Build One (2026) (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/zero-based-budget-excel.html)
Q: What does zero-based budgeting mean?
A: Zero-based budgeting is a budgeting method where every dollar of income is assigned a specific job — spending, saving, investing, or debt payoff — until the difference between income and total allocations equals zero. The method doesn't mean spending zero dollars; it means leaving zero dollars unassigned at the end of the allocation.
Q: Is zero-based budgeting good for beginners?
A: Zero-based budgeting works well for beginners because it forces a decision on every dollar rather than relying on vague guidelines. The main risk is creating too many categories or underestimating variable expenses like groceries and utilities. Starting with 8 to 12 categories and adjusting after two or three months is the most sustainable approach.
Q: How is zero-based budgeting different from the 50/30/20 rule?
A: The 50/30/20 rule is a high-level allocation framework — 50% of income to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to savings and debt. Zero-based budgeting is a line-by-line method where every dollar is assigned to a specific category. The two can work together: 50/30/20 sets the overall allocation, and zero-based budgeting fills in the specific categories within each bucket.
Q: Can you do zero-based budgeting in Google Sheets?
A: Yes. Every formula used in a zero-based budget works identically in Google Sheets, including SUM, variance calculations, and conditional formatting. The only meaningful difference is slightly different menu paths for features like Named Ranges and Tables, but the underlying logic is the same.
Q: What's the biggest reason zero-based budgets fail?
A: The biggest reason zero-based budgets fail is category drift — starting with a clean list of categories and letting it balloon to 20+ categories over a few months. The second biggest reason is formula breakage between monthly sheets, where carrying the structure forward introduces errors that aren't caught until the numbers stop reconciling. Both are architecture problems, not discipline problems.
Q: Do I need a budgeting app if I have a zero-based budget spreadsheet?
A: No. A well-built zero-based budget spreadsheet replaces the core functionality of most budgeting apps — category tracking, variance reporting, and month-over-month comparison. Apps add value when real-time bank syncing matters or when sharing finances with someone who won't open a spreadsheet.

### FAQ — First-Time Homebuyer Mistakes: The Mortgage Math Most Buyers Skip (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/first-time-homebuyer-mistakes.html)
Q: What is the biggest mistake first-time homebuyers make?
A: The biggest first-time homebuyer mistake is anchoring on the monthly mortgage payment instead of the true monthly cost of homeownership. Principal and interest is typically 55% to 65% of what you'll actually pay each month once you include property taxes, insurance, PMI, HOA fees, utilities, and maintenance reserves. Budgets built on the lender's quoted payment are structurally incomplete.
Q: How much should first-time buyers budget for closing costs?
A: Closing costs typically range from 2% to 5% of the home's purchase price. On a $350,000 home, that's $7,000 to $17,500 on top of the down payment. The biggest line items are loan origination fees, title insurance, appraisal, prepaid property taxes and insurance, and recording fees. First-time buyers should budget 3% as a starting assumption and refine the number when they receive a Loan Estimate from their lender.
Q: Is the 28/36 rule still a reliable affordability guideline?
A: The 28/36 rule is a reasonable starting point but misleads many modern first-time buyers. It uses gross income, which overstates available funds for self-employed buyers, dual-income households, anyone with student loans, and buyers in high-cost-of-living areas. A more conservative framework uses take-home pay after retirement contributions, health insurance, childcare, and existing debt — then caps total housing costs at 35% of the remainder.
Q: How long do you need to stay in a home for buying to beat renting?
A: The break-even point for buying versus renting typically falls between 5 and 10 years, but depends heavily on local rent-to-price ratios, expected home value appreciation, your down payment's opportunity cost in alternative investments, and whether a renter would actually invest the monthly difference. Under 5 years, renting almost always wins after closing and selling costs. Past 10 years, buying usually wins in most markets.
Q: What is the difference between the interest rate and the APR on a mortgage?
A: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing the principal. The APR (annual percentage rate) includes the interest rate plus lender fees like origination, discount points, and mortgage insurance expressed as an annualized cost. APR is always higher than the base interest rate and is the better number to use when comparing loan offers, because it captures the full cost of the loan.
Q: How much impact do extra mortgage payments actually have?
A: Extra principal payments have outsized impact because of how amortization front-loads interest in the early years. On a $300,000 mortgage at 6.75% over 30 years, adding $100 per month in extra principal saves approximately $54,000 in interest and pays off the loan 4 years early. Adding $250 per month saves roughly $108,000 and pays off the loan 8 years early.

### FAQ — How to Track Etsy and Gumroad Income in Notion (Without a Spreadsheet Mess) (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/track-etsy-gumroad-income-notion.html)
Q: Why is my Etsy or Gumroad payout different from what I earned?
A: Each platform deducts its own fees before the money reaches your bank — Etsy takes listing, transaction, and payment-processing fees, and Gumroad takes a flat percentage plus processing. The deposit you see is net of those cuts, so tracking only your bank deposits hides what you grossed and what you paid in fees. Recording gross, fees, and net separately for each sale shows the real picture.
Q: How do I track income from multiple platforms in one place?
A: Use a single income log with a Platform property (Etsy, Gumroad, YouTube, client work, and so on) and separate fields for gross amount, platform fees, and net. Filtering or grouping by platform then shows which channel actually earns the most after fees, not just which one deposits the most.
Q: Do Etsy and Gumroad pay out on the same schedule?
A: No. Payout timing differs by platform and by your settings — deposits can be daily, weekly, or on a delay, and a sale made in one month can land in your bank the next. Logging income by the date of the sale rather than the date of the deposit keeps your monthly totals accurate.
Q: How much should I set aside for taxes?
A: A common rule of thumb is to set aside roughly 25–30 percent of net self-employment income for taxes, but the right number depends on your total income, location, and filing situation. This is general information, not tax advice — confirm your own number with a qualified tax professional.

### FAQ — How to Plan a Year of Content Without Burning Out (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/how-to-plan-content-year-without-burnout.html)
Q: How many themes should I plan for a year of content?
A: Two or three is the right number. Fewer and the year of content feels too narrow to develop a real body of work; more and the content stops cohering. Themes are territories, not topics — broad enough to live in for months, specific enough to give the work identity.
Q: What does the 80% capacity rule mean?
A: It means planning content production at 80% of your measured weekly capacity, not 100%. If you can produce three posts a week on average, plan for 2.4 — call it ten posts a month, not twelve. The remaining 20% is slack to absorb bad weeks, surprises, and revision time. Plans built at 100% capacity collapse the first time real life happens.
Q: What is the difference between cadence and capacity?
A: Capacity is how much content you can sustainably produce in an average week. Cadence is the rhythm at which content publishes. Cadence has to be downstream of capacity — set capacity first, then choose a cadence that fits. Setting cadence first and forcing capacity to match is how creators end up burning out by month two.
Q: How often should I revise an annual content plan?
A: A monthly review of what shipped, what did not, and what is still relevant keeps the plan alive. A quarterly revision adjusts themes and topics based on what is working. The plan exists to serve the work — when the plan stops serving the work, change the plan.
Q: What is the difference between a content theme and a content topic?
A: Themes are broad directions ("how creators build sustainable income"). Topics are specific pieces inside a theme ("five ways to monetize a newsletter"). Themes change slowly across a year. Topics get filled in week by week. Without themes, every post is a one-off and the body of work does not compound.

### FAQ — The Real Reason Most Solo Creators Stay Stuck Under $5K/Month (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/why-solo-creators-stay-stuck-under-5k.html)
Q: Why doesn't more marketing usually break the $5K plateau?
A: Without back-end systems, marketing pushes get traffic to a leaky funnel. Without lead capture, follow-up sequences, or proper customer tracking, the spike monetizes 1–2% and fades. You can do this every month for a year and the baseline is unchanged. The fix isn't usually more marketing — it's a tighter back end so marketing efforts compound instead of evaporating.
Q: When should a solo creator start building business systems?
A: Before you need them. Systems aren't a thing you graduate to once you're big — they're a thing you build to get big. The creator who waits until $10K/month spends years stuck under that ceiling because the lack of infrastructure is what's keeping them under it. A simple lead tracker for fifty leads is overkill until you have five hundred and wish you'd been tracking them all along.
Q: What are the five operations a real creator business runs?
A: Lead and customer tracking, pipeline management, financial visibility, content and product pipeline, and launch and offer rotation. A creator running all five — even at a basic level — is in a different business than one running on attention and recall. The plateau breaks because the underlying capacity to handle growth is finally there.
Q: How do you know you've hit the operator transition?
A: The work feels less frantic. Decisions get faster because the data is right there. Marketing efforts compound instead of evaporating, because the leads are tracked and followed up with. Launches are easier because the pipeline of products is already built. Pricing changes are confident because the margin data is visible.
Q: Do I need enterprise software for systems like this?
A: No. The right setup is a structured Notion workspace, a few spreadsheets, and a process you actually follow. Enterprise CRMs at $50–200/month are overkill for a solo creator and often introduce more friction than they remove. Lightweight templates that match how creators actually work outperform expensive software for businesses at this scale.

### FAQ — How to Launch a Digital Product Without an Audience (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/how-to-launch-digital-product-without-audience.html)
Q: Can you really launch a product without an email list?
A: Yes. The mental shift is launching into an audience that already exists somewhere else, not building one from scratch. Marketplaces, search engines, AI assistants, and topical communities all have audiences you can plug into immediately. First launches that ship into Etsy or Notion Marketplace can hit a few sales in the first week. First launches that wait for an email list often take two years and never happen.
Q: What are the four entry points for an audience-less launch?
A: Marketplaces with native traffic (Etsy, Gumroad, Notion Marketplace), search engines (well-written content about the problem your product solves), AI assistants (ChatGPT and Claude get asked product questions constantly — your product page can be cited if it's structured for it), and topical communities (subreddits, Discord servers, Slack workspaces where you've established credibility).
Q: How much should a first launch cost?
A: For digital products with no audience or trust foundation, $9–$29 is a trust-friendly range. Higher prices work but require trust you don't have yet. The right first launch is smaller in scope than feels comfortable, solving a specific problem you can describe in one sentence, and easy to deliver and support. The flagship $200 product can come second.
Q: Should I launch on Etsy or my own website first?
A: Both, ideally. Etsy gives you immediate access to existing buyer-intent traffic and trust infrastructure. Your own product page gives you the canonical version with full control over presentation, schema, and direct customer relationships. The strongest audience-less launches use a marketplace + own-site + one community combination.
Q: How long does it take to see results from an audience-less launch?
A: First-day traffic is going to be modest by definition — there's no list to email. The first 30 days post-launch matter more than launch day itself. Watch where traffic is actually coming from (often surprising), talk to the first ten buyers (highest-quality market research you'll ever do), iterate the product page based on real signal, and add a new entry point in week three. Compounding distribution starts here, not on day one.

### FAQ — The 50/30/20 Rule Is Outdated — Here's What Actually Works in 2026 (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/50-30-20-rule-outdated-budgeting-2026.html)
Q: Why is the 50/30/20 rule considered outdated?
A: It was introduced in Elizabeth Warren's 2005 book All Your Worth, when housing, healthcare, student debt, childcare, and basic digital infrastructure consumed less of the average household's after-tax income. In 2026, the "needs" half of the split is closer to 65–70% for many households, which means the math breaks. The rule isn't wrong as a direction — it's just hard to apply when the input numbers don't fit the boxes.
Q: What budgeting frameworks work better than 50/30/20?
A: Several modern alternatives: zero-based budgeting (every dollar gets a job), pay-yourself-first budgeting (savings come off the top), reverse budgeting (track first, plan second), values-based budgeting (fund what genuinely matters, ruthlessly cut what doesn't), and hybrid percentage frameworks (60/20/20 or 50/20/30 depending on income level and life stage). None is universally better — each fits a different situation.
Q: Is zero-based budgeting better than 50/30/20?
A: Different tools for different problems. 50/30/20 is a high-level allocation framework — easy to teach, easy to remember, useful as a starting model. Zero-based budgeting is a line-by-line method where every dollar is assigned to a specific category. Zero-based produces more accurate spending data; 50/30/20 produces an easier mental model. Many households use both — 50/30/20 for the broad allocation, zero-based for the actual line items inside each category.
Q: What is values-based budgeting?
A: A framework where you identify the few categories that genuinely matter to your household — say, education, travel, and retirement — and structure the budget so those categories are well-funded while ruthlessly cutting categories that don't align. The advantage is meaningfulness — your budget reflects what you actually care about. The disadvantage is that it requires real reflection on values, which most household budgeting tools don't surface.
Q: Should I use percentages or dollar amounts in my budget?
A: For households where the same percentage allocation produces wildly different outcomes at different income levels, dollar amounts work better. Some costs are fixed in dollar terms regardless of income — utilities, insurance, basic groceries. A household earning $40K and a household earning $80K don't pay double for those. Modern budgeting tends to combine both: dollar amounts for fixed costs, percentages for discretionary buckets.

### FAQ — How Much House Can You Actually Afford? (The Honest Math) (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/how-much-house-can-you-actually-afford.html)
Q: What costs do lenders not include in home affordability calculations?
A: Lender PITI calculations capture principal, interest, property taxes, and homeowners insurance. They miss maintenance and repairs (1–4% of home value per year), utilities ($300–600+ per month for a typical single-family home), property tax escalation, insurance premium escalation, HOA dues and special assessments, closing costs (2–5% of purchase price), and moving and immediate setup costs ($5,000–15,000 above the purchase price). The real cost of homeownership is often 30–50% higher than the mortgage payment alone.
Q: What is the difference between front-end ratio and back-end ratio?
A: Front-end ratio (housing ratio) is total monthly housing cost divided by gross monthly income — most lenders look for 28% or below. Back-end ratio (debt-to-income, or DTI) is total monthly debt obligations divided by gross monthly income — typically 36% or below for conventional loans, sometimes higher for specific programs. Both ratios use gross income, not take-home pay, which is the first place the lender's affordability number diverges from real affordability.
Q: Why does gross income vs take-home pay matter for affordability?
A: Lenders calculate ratios against gross income — your pay before taxes, healthcare premiums, retirement contributions, and other deductions. A household with $100K gross might take home $70–75K. The lender's "affordable" payment can be a substantial portion of your real take-home pay, even when it fits the lender's formula. Real affordability uses take-home, not gross.
Q: How much house can I afford on take-home pay?
A: A more honest version of the standard rule for many households: keep total housing costs (PITI + maintenance reserve + utilities + HOA) at or below 30–35% of take-home pay, not gross. This produces a smaller affordable home than the 28%-of-gross rule but leaves room for the rest of the household budget — savings, retirement, education, healthcare, emergencies, and discretionary spending. The right number varies enormously by situation.
Q: What is the 28% rule for housing costs?
A: The classic advice — keep your housing payment at or below 28% of gross income. It's a useful starting point but has the same blind spots as the lender's calculation. 28% applies to gross income (pre-tax). On take-home pay, 28% of gross is often closer to 38–40%. The 28% covers PITI, not the broader costs of homeownership. If real homeownership costs run 30–50% higher than PITI, then a 28% PITI ratio means actual housing cost is closer to 36–42% of gross — roughly half of take-home.

### FAQ — Building the Universal Recipe Scaler: A Local-First, Ad-Free Kitchen Utility (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/blog/building-the-universal-recipe-scaler.html)
Q: Is the Universal Recipe Scaler free?
A: Yes — completely free, with no signup, no email gate, and no premium tier. It's hosted on GitHub Pages and the entire tool runs in your browser.
Q: Does it work offline?
A: Once the page has loaded, yes — there's no backend to call. If you load it on a flight or with bad Wi-Fi, it keeps working. localStorage means your last recipe stays saved between sessions even without an internet connection.
Q: Why can't I paste the full recipe with instructions?
A: The tool intentionally only scales ingredient lists. Pasting the full recipe (with cooking times and temperatures) would risk the math engine scaling cooking times — "bake for 30 minutes" becoming "bake for 60 minutes" when you double a recipe. Restricting input to the ingredient list keeps the conversions accurate.
Q: Why does it convert to kg/L automatically but leave temperatures alone?
A: Temperatures and dimensions (inches, centimeters) don't scale with recipe size. If you double a recipe, the oven still bakes at the same temperature for the same time. The tool ignores those values entirely and only scales ingredient quantities. Auto-converting grams to kilograms above 1000g is purely a presentation choice — easier to read 1.2 kg than 1200 g.
Q: Does it store my recipes? Where does my data go?
A: The tool uses browser localStorage, which lives on your device. Nothing is sent to a server. If you clear your browser data, the saved recipe is gone. If you switch devices, the recipe doesn't transfer — it's truly local. There's no account system because there's nothing to account for.
Q: Can I use it on my phone?
A: Yes. The interface is responsive and works on phones, tablets, and laptops. The interactive prep checklist is especially useful on a phone propped up next to the cutting board while you're actually cooking.
Q: What's the technology behind it?
A: Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. No backend. Single-page utility under 100 KB total. Hosted on GitHub Pages. JSON-LD WebApplication schema for search engines. The whole thing is intentionally minimal — the goal is to be the fastest thing you can find when you need to scale a recipe.

### FAQ — Chinese zodiac art — all 12 animals (https://builtbyjoshstudio.com/collections/chinese-zodiac-art.html)
Q: Where can I buy Chinese zodiac art prints online?
A: The full Chinese zodiac art print collection is available to buy direct on this site. All 12 animals are available as instant digital download bundles — you check out securely on builtbyjoshstudio.com, download the high-resolution files immediately, and print them at home or at a local print shop. The Built by Josh Studio Etsy shop carries individual prints and other studio work, not these bundles. No physical product is shipped.
Q: What Chinese zodiac animal am I?
A: Your Chinese zodiac animal is determined by your birth year. The 12-year cycle is Rat, Ox, Tiger, Rabbit, Dragon, Snake, Horse, Goat, Monkey, Rooster, Dog, and Pig. For example, if you were born in 1988 or 2000 you're a Dragon; if born in 1990 or 2002 you're a Horse. Note that the Chinese zodiac year starts at Lunar New Year (late January or February), so if you were born in January or early February, your animal may be from the previous year.
Q: What art style is the Chinese zodiac collection?
A: The entire Chinese zodiac collection is rendered in a hyper-realistic dark fantasy style called the Lunar Guardians series. Each animal is reimagined as a mythic guardian figure with cinematic lighting, armor-like detailing, and rich atmospheric depth. The style is consistent across all 12 animals, making them work well as a cohesive set.
Q: Is Chinese zodiac art a good Lunar New Year gift?
A: Yes. Gifting someone art of their Chinese zodiac animal during Lunar New Year is a personal, culturally meaningful gesture. You can purchase the digital file and print and frame it before giving, or forward the download link directly. The Year of the Snake (2025) and Year of the Horse (2026) bundles are particularly timely options.
Q: How many prints are in each Chinese zodiac bundle?
A: Each animal listing is a bundle that includes multiple art prints of the same animal. All bundles are priced at $6.99 and include high-resolution files ready for printing at standard frame sizes.
Q: Can I use these Chinese zodiac prints commercially or resell them?
A: No. All prints are licensed for personal use only — printing for your own home, office, or as a personal gift. Commercial use including reselling, redistribution, print-on-demand, or merchandising is not permitted under the license.

Q: What is the Year of the Snake 2025 and Year of the Horse 2026?
A: 2025 is the Year of the Snake in the Chinese zodiac, which began at Lunar New Year in late January 2025. 2026 is the Year of the Horse, beginning at Lunar New Year in February 2026. Both animals are available as Lunar Guardians art print bundles in the Built by Josh Studio Chinese zodiac collection.
